title: Balanced Equation
summary: A balanced equation is a chemical equation with equal numbers of each atom on both sides — obeying conservation of mass. It is the precise recipe of a reaction.

parts: The written form of conservation of mass
processes: Adjusting coefficients until the sides match
plainLanguageExplanation: A balanced equation is a chemical equation in which the number of each kind of atom is the same on both sides of the arrow. Look at 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Left side: the 2 in front of H₂ means two H₂ units, so 4 hydrogens; plus O₂ gives 2 oxygens. Right side: 2H₂O means two water molecules — 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens. Every atom matches. Balanced. Why does this matter? Because reactions obey conservation of mass — atoms are never created or destroyed. An equation with mismatched atoms would be describing something impossible. Balancing is done by adjusting the coefficients — the numbers in front of the formulas — never by changing the subscripts inside the formulas. Changing a subscript would change the substance itself. So the recipe is: count the atoms, then tune the coefficients until both sides match. A balanced equation is a true recipe — it tells you exactly how much of each substance reacts and forms.

whyItMatters: Balancing equations is the central skill of chemistry — it is how chemists write reactions truthfully, predict quantities, and respect the law of conservation of mass. A balanced equation is the difference between a correct recipe and a fictional one.
tagline: The true recipe of a reaction
didYouKnow: The phrase 'atoms are conserved' means a properly balanced equation is like an accounting sheet — every atom that goes in on the left is accounted for on the right, nothing lost, nothing invented.
compareReason: Balancing is the skill and conservation of mass is the law it obeys — comparing them shows why the written equation must always match reality.
